extracted.intended_audience: early-career job seekers and young professionals (especially those pursuing media, fashion, retail, and entry-level roles)
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of anecdotal interview failures illustrating practical do's and don'ts for job-seekers (timing, preparation, safety, demeanor, follow-up) across media, fashion, retail, and service roles. Useful as informal guidance for preparing and surviving a variety of interview formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal safety in informal/trial interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid unsafe or unvetted interview situations (e.g., Craigslist gigs, one-night trials at private apartments) where you may be alone with strangers or exposed to inappropriate conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an interview or trial puts you in an isolated private space or with someone behaving inappropriately (shirtless host, sexual comments, demands), leave and decline the position. Prioritize safety over getting a gig; trust instincts and notify contacts if you feel threatened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and prepare for stress/’bar raiser’ interviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Some employers use deliberate stress interviews or 'bar raisers'—interviewers whose role is to challenge you aggressively and test cultural fit under pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know whether the company uses stress interviews (Amazon's 'bar raiser' cited). Practice staying composed under interruptions and brainteasers; focus on process and calm communication rather than trying to 'beat' the trick question. Recognize the tactic and avoid taking rude behavior personally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know role- and industry-specific facts (brands, designers, products)
rubrics_metrics.description: For roles in fashion, retail, food/service, and media, interviewers may ask for favorite brands, designers, or product knowledge; blanking can signal lack of industry fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare concrete examples (favorite brands, designers, outlets) beyond generic answers. For fashion roles, be ready for designer trivia (e.g., 'Who is the designer of Lanvin?'). For service roles, review menu/booze/terminology likely to appear on tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for case and format-specific interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain employers (consulting, some corporate roles) use case interviews or other specialized formats that require practiced analytical frameworks rather than general chat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the format in advance and practice cases; if you've never done a case interview, familiarize yourself with the structure so you don't 'stumble through' under timed conditions. Use mock interviews to build fluency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuality and calendar accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrive on time and double-check interview times/locations—mistakes in scheduling (mixing up times) can lead to rushed, sweaty, and unsuccessful interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm time zones, calendar invites, and travel time; 'pay attention to your Google Calendar'—set reminders and allow extra travel time. If you are late, apologize concisely and refocus; avoid scrambling excuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate domain knowledge and ability to impact the role
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviewers may probe how you'll actually influence the role and ask think-on-your-feet questions about impact, strategy, or metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be ready with concrete examples of how your experience maps to the job and how you would measure impact. If pushed on specifics, use relevant buzzwords carefully but prioritize concrete examples and logical reasoning over vague platitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial-shift / on-the-job test readiness and resilience
rubrics_metrics.description: Trial days (e.g., restaurant, barista, photography trial) can include chaotic real-world scenarios, abrupt firings, and requests to perform menial tasks under pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to handle messy, high-pressure, or humiliating moments professionally (mop spills, pitch in). Observe workplace norms; if a manager behaves abusively, weigh whether the job environment is acceptable but maintain composure during the assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for rapid-fire or obscure factual questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviewers may ask quick, seemingly trivial factual questions to test composure and cultural fit (e.g., hometown descriptions, favorite musicians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare concise, positive, and non-embarrassing responses to common personal and behavioral prompts. Avoid answers that could harm your impression (overly odd or niche preferences) and practice speaking about yourself clearly under mild pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid résumé clichés and be specific/honest
rubrics_metrics.description: Vague or clichéd résumé language (e.g., 'incredibly motivated') invites harsh critique and undermines credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete accomplishments and metrics rather than platitudes. Be honest about qualifications; avoid filler phrases. Expect recruiters to scrutinize and question vague claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send sincere follow-up/thank-you notes
rubrics_metrics.description: A thoughtful, honest thank-you note after an interview can positively influence a recruiter's perception and even revive opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write brief, genuine follow-ups highlighting appreciation and any clarifying points. Personal, reflective notes can stick with interviewers (example: recruiter pinned a thank-you card and later recommended the candidate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate nonverbal behavior and handshake etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Body language (handshake strength, eye contact, composure) affects impressions—overly strong or odd gestures can derail rapport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match handshake firmness to context (firm but not crushing), maintain professional posture, and avoid nervous or attention-grabbing physical antics (double finger-guns, etc.). Practice typical professional greetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only claim demonstrable skills (don’t overstate language/technical ability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boasting 'conversational' ability or other skills you cannot demonstrate in conversation can backfire if interviewers test you unexpectedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you list a skill (language, software), be ready to show it or to use it in the interview. Err on the side of modesty or qualify the level accurately (e.g., 'basic conversational French' with examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify interview details: role, level, location, and interviewer identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistakes happen (being brought in for the wrong seniority level or going to the wrong campus bookstore); lack of clarity can lead to embarrassment and automatic mismatch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm the exact job title, required qualifications, interview location/address, and who will be interviewing you ahead of time. If something seems off during check-in, politely clarify rather than assuming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid discussing or competing with personal contacts/exes during the process
rubrics_metrics.description: Encountering personal acquaintances (exes, friends) in waiting rooms or applying for the same jobs can be distracting and affect performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain professionalism, minimize interaction in the recruitment setting, and mentally prepare to focus on your interview rather than social dynamics in the waiting area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence after rejection / consider reapplying
rubrics_metrics.description: A bad interview or an abrasive interviewer doesn't always reflect the entire organization; reapplying or staying in touch can lead to later opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If rejected, consider polite reapplication, especially if the interviewer was known to be abrasive or subsequently removed. Learn from the experience and try again when a better-fitting opening arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research employer portfolio and avoid praising competitors by mistake
rubrics_metrics.description: Complimenting competitors or misidentifying which brands belong to an employer signals lack of preparation and can make you appear uninformed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the company's brands, recent work, and competitive landscape so compliments are accurate and relevant. When in doubt, frame answers around the employer's publicly known strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ready for role-specific written or product-knowledge tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Some entry-level/service positions include written tests or quizzes about product knowledge (e.g., top-shelf spirits, menu items).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For service and retail jobs, review common product names and terminology; for editorial roles, familiarize yourself with the publication's style and coverage. Small knowledge gaps on tests can be disqualifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirm that interview expectations align with your qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally you'll be interviewed for a role requiring far more senior qualifications than you possess (e.g., JD required for senior management).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before attending, check the job posting and, if unclear, ask the recruiter to confirm seniority level and required credentials. If unexpectedly interviewed for a higher-level role, be honest and treat it as a practice opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize abusive or discriminatory interviewer behavior and set boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviewers may behave abusively, make discriminatory remarks, or ask inappropriate personal questions (e.g., comments about women's bodies or demands about hair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You are not obliged to tolerate harassment; if comments cross professional lines, consider ending the interview, documenting what happened, and reporting it to HR or the recruiting platform. Preserve safety and dignity first.
